newsitem.title: ISRAEL: New site aims to bring Internet to family audience.
newsitem.headline: New site aims to bring Internet to family audience.

text.p: For people who find browsing the Internet technologically challenging, help is coming in the form of a new site launched in the United States on Monday that mimics the layout of a theme park.

VCOT, which stands for Virtual Community of Tomorrow, is an Internet site comprising 20 "pavillions" offering everything from Reuters news to on-line art exhibits, medical and health information, games and other family fare features.
The centre-piece is the pavillion containing a multimedia version of the Funk & Wagnalls Encyclopedia with animated diagrams and sound recordings.

Harry Fox, whose Israel-based company Community Network Systems (CNS) developed and is marketing the site, says VCOT is aimed squarely at people who don't take spreadsheets home from the office at night but use their PC strictly for entertainment.
"We are targetting the site to families," said Fox. "We are trying to provide affordable content as opposed to overpriced CD-ROMs."

VCOT offers a visually compelling site, whose animation moves smoothly over the 28 kilobit-per-second modems attached to most PCs now and requires minimal on-board software from the user. Its content is taken from other providers but, says Fox, unlike other sites it is re-configured into its own user-friendly format.
CNS has made no tecnological innovations in the realm of Internet transmission.
"We use off-the-shelf tools," Fox told Reuters. "We build custom utilities. We have talented people who know how to exploit the technology to the limits of the envelope."

Fox is convinced the site will be compelling enough to charge a subscription fee at least for the Fund & Wagnalls pavillion of $29.95. Other parts of VCOT like Reuters are free, some being advertising-supported.

Fox said he expects VCOT to help broaden Internet usage by giving ordinary people a good reason to go on-line. An early player in the U.S. CD-ROM business, Fox says the disks never achieved their potential because of high costs and distribution problems.
"The Internet affords the opportunity to fulfill the lost promise of the CD-ROM," he said.
Fox came to Israel originally to develop CD-ROMs and has stayed on to build websites and other software projects because of the software talent available.
"The skill level of the people is so high that if you have a clear business plan you can have two to three times the productivity of the rest of the world," Fox said.
VCOT will be available directly by downloading (the site is www:VCOT.com), but Fox hopes to lure most users through bundling agreements with PC makers and Internet service providers.

"The way we hope to get our first one million VCOT users is to have the hardware manufacturers pay for one-year subscriptions," said Fox. He said CNS was in advanced talks with Hewlett-Packard and Prodigy among others.
Fox is aiming for an installed base of one million by the end of the year because that will give him the base for advertising revenues and sponsorships.

From there CNS will be looking to set up joint ventures for VCOT in eight other countries over the next two years, each with a mix of worldwide and local content. Fox also plans to start building intranet sites for school systems and a site for lawyers, doctors and other professionals offering on-line services.
